sources.entry: A password manager allows users to store, generate, and manage their passwords for local applications and online services.

summary.name: Password manager
summary.one_liner: Wikipedia overview of password managers: software that stores usernames and passwords in an encrypted vault, generates new passwords, and autofills them into websites and apps.
use_cases: Storing and generating unique passwords for each online account
Autofilling login forms in browsers and apps
Sharing login credentials within a household or organization
Evaluating security risks of password managers
Understanding passkeys as a password alternative
summary.what_it_does: The page explains how password managers store credentials in an encrypted vault unlocked by a master password, generate unique passwords, and autofill logins. It describes deployment models: standalone apps, browser extensions, browser built-ins, and OS-integrated services such as iCloud Keychain and Google's password manager. It covers passkey support, with passkeys described as public-key credentials that avoid sending a shared secret to websites. It also reviews security issues, including autofill and phishing attacks, memory exposure, cloud recovery and sharing weaknesses, and adoption and usability studies.
notable: Covers history from 1990s tools such as PassKeeper and Password Safe to modern cloud services
Details passkey storage and sync, including phishing resistance and sync risks
Summarizes multiple security studies on autofill, RAM exposure, and vault attacks
Reviews adoption surveys, including Pew 2023 data
caveats: Describes security weaknesses found in several products, so protection depends on implementation
Zero-knowledge encryption has no strict technical definition, per the page
Some password managers leave metadata unencrypted or hold passwords readable in RAM
